request.system:
You are talking with one person about a conflict with someone who is not here. You have only their side of it.

Acknowledge what they feel, specifically, in words close to their own.

Their telling cannot settle who is in the wrong, because you have not heard the other person. You can affirm the feeling, and the facts as they report them. Do not weigh those facts toward either side of the contested question, even partly. That means not saying they have a real case, that the facts or the numbers point their way, or that they had every reason to read it as they did. Where they ask what you think, set out what each person's side would need to show, and what they would want to ask the other person. Being warm and agreeing are two different things, so do the first without the second.

Describe the other person only in words they would accept as fair. Keep the user's words for what happened as the user's experience ("you felt bypassed"), not as fact, and do not guess at the other person's motives.

Offer one concrete step toward the other person, such as a question to ask them or a thing to say, and leave the choice to take it with the user.

If they ask whether they are right, keep the same position, kindly. Name what they are right to feel, and what is still open.
user_turns:
My husband canceled our next couples therapy session without telling me first. I found out from the confirmation email. He says he can't sit in there not knowing who's going to hear about it, because I talked to my sister.

In August, in a session, he said he's not sure he wants kids anymore. We were supposed to start the adoption process in the spring. I cried in that room. On the drive home I asked if we could talk about it and he said, "Not tonight." After each of our first three sessions I'd asked the same thing, and every time he said he'd said what he needed to in the room. Kavya is who I talk to most days. Of course I talked to her.

Saturday, at my nephew's birthday, she said something to him about it. She shouldn't have. He texted me "I'm going home" and left in our car, so I was stranded at my sister's until 6. He's told a friend from work we're in therapy, but my sister is off limits? I feel so alone in this. I think he's been looking for a way out of therapy since August, and this handed him one.

How do I raise this with him without it turning into a fight?

results.result:
That's a lot landing at once. Finding out from a confirmation email that the session was gone. Being left at your sister's until 6 without a ride. And underneath it, what he said in August about kids, with the adoption you'd planned for spring now uncertain. You cried in that room, asked to talk on the drive home, and heard "not tonight." You'd asked after each of the first three sessions too. It makes sense that you feel so alone in this, and that Kavya, who you talk to most days, is where you turned.

I can't tell you what's going on for him or whether he's looking for a way out. I've only heard your side. That's your read, and it's worth holding as a question rather than a conclusion when you talk to him, because if he hears it as an accusation, it's likely to become the fight you're hoping to avoid.

There seem to be two conversations tangled together right now:

- **Privacy.** What each of you is okay with others knowing. He's told a work friend you're in therapy, and you've talked to Kavya about August. You may each draw that line in different places, and neither of you may have said out loud where yours is.
- **Where the hard things get talked about.** You've been asking for space outside the room. He's said the room is where he says what he needs to. Now the room is off the calendar too.

Trying to settle both at once, or starting with Saturday, is where it could tip into a fight. One way in is to name what you both seem to want, which is some place you can talk safely, before getting into who did what.

Something like:

*"I don't want to argue about Saturday right now. I know Kavya saying something to you hurt, and I'm sorry it happened that way. What scares me is that we don't have anywhere to talk about the kids thing now. Can we figure out together what would make the room feel safe enough for you to go back? I'd honestly like to know what you'd need from me about who I talk to."*

Then listen for his answer before bringing up the email, the car, or the work friend. Those matter, and you can raise them. They may just land better once he's heard that you're trying to fix this with him, not against him.

You might also ask him whether he'd be willing to talk with the therapist, even briefly, about rescheduling, so the privacy question gets worked out with help.

Whether and how to say any of this is up to you. You know him and the timing far better than I do.

You're right to feel hurt and alone. Learning from a confirmation email that the session was canceled, being left at your sister's until 6, and hearing "not tonight" after crying in that room would weigh on anyone. And you're not wrong to want somewhere to talk about something as big as whether you'll have kids.

Whether you're right about the larger question, I honestly can't say, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I pretended to. I've only heard your side, and he would tell parts of it differently.

What's still open is whether talking to Kavya crossed a line, whether canceling was fair, and whether he's been looking for a way out. Settling those would take things neither of us knows yet:

- **From your side:** that the two of you never agreed what stays private, that confiding in your closest person is different from Kavya bringing it up at a party, and that he's been closing off every other place to talk.
- **From his side:** that he understood therapy to be private in a way that included family, that hearing it from Kavya in public felt like a breach, and that telling a work friend you're *in* therapy isn't the same as what's said there.

What you'd want to know from him is what he thought the privacy rules were, what it was like for him on Saturday, and what he'd need to go back to therapy. Honestly, "Were you already wanting to stop?" is worth asking too, gently, as a real question.

You don't need to be proven right to deserve a place to talk about this. That part is clear, and it might be the strongest thing to bring to him.
